newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Britain says to stay in UN industrial agency.
newsitem.headline: Britain says to stay in UN industrial agency.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government announced on Thursday it was withdrawing a threat by its Conservative predecessor to withdraw from the United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO).

The announcement was made by Secretary of State for International Development Clare Short to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan and other ministers attending a session of the world body's Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC).

The Vienna-based UNIDO, she told reporters later, had undertaken fundamental reform of itself and was working to refocus activities "into high priority areas which match the changing needs of developing countries, especially in Africa.
"We believe that a leaner, refocused and more effective UNIDO is needed to assist developing countries to industrialise.

"Poor countries need cost-free and independent advice of the kind which United Nations agencies have the mandate and the capacity to provide," Short said she had told a breakfast meeting hosted by Annan for the ministers.

The announcement follows Britain's return on July 1 to the the U.N.'s Paris-based Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO), from which it withdrew more than a decade ago under the administration of Margaret Thatcher.

The former Conservative government, following a lead by the United States which has now left UNIDO, announced last December that it would end British membership at the end of 1997 unless there had been good progress in overall U.N. reform.

Short, a long-time campaigner for development causes, said the new government of Prime Minister Tony Blair "wants to work constructively within UNIDO and with all our partners in order to promote the process of internal change.
"A more effective U.N. is essential if we are to achieve our goal of poverty eradication," she said.
UNIDO, originally set up in 1967, is responsible for promoting and accelerating industrialisation in developing countries to help them break away from dependence on commodities and primary products.
As a member, Britain makes a compulsory contribution of some $6.6 million (four million sterling) a year, or 7.4 per cent of the body's current budget.
